title: Vertebrates & Invertebrates
subtitle: One bone decides which of the two halves an animal is in.
objectives: Explain what makes an animal a vertebrate
Name the five vertebrate classes and one feature of each
Name six invertebrate groups and give an example of each
Explain the difference between an exoskeleton and an endoskeleton
Explain why arthropods are the largest animal group

cards.title: The whole animal kingdom splits on one question
cards.text: Does it have a backbone? That single answer sorts every animal on earth into one of two piles.

cards.title: Vertebrate or invertebrate
cards.text: It is not an even split. One side is vastly bigger than the other, and it is not the side you would guess.
points: **Vertebrate** — has a backbone. Five classes.
**Invertebrate** — no backbone. Many more groups.
**About 95% of animal species** are invertebrates.
**Week 1 called it the vertebral column.** Same bone.

cards.title: One feature identifies each class
cards.text: Tap through. Several quiz questions come from this.

options: Hair or fur, and milk for the young
question.explain: Hair and milk. Birds lay hard-shelled eggs, and fish have the gills and scales.

cards.title: Warm-blooded or cold-blooded
cards.text: Only two of the five classes hold their own temperature. The other three take whatever the surroundings give them.
points: **Warm-blooded:** birds and mammals only.
**Cold-blooded:** fish, amphibians, reptiles.
**Cold-blooded means the outside decides**, not that they are cold.
**A lizard on a hot rock** is warmer than you are.

cards.title: Holding your temperature costs food
cards.text: Staying at 37 °C all day and night is expensive. That is why warm-blooded animals eat far more than cold-blooded ones their size.
points: **A snake can eat once a month.**
**You cannot go a day without noticing.**
**You are paying for the temperature.**
**Both work.** They are different strategies.

question.explain: Birds and mammals. The other three take their temperature from their surroundings.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Five classes done. Part 2 is the other 95% of the animal kingdom. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Almost every animal is in this half
cards.text: Vertebrates get the attention because we are one. By number of species, they are a rounding error.

cards.title: Six groups you have to know
cards.text: Tap through each one. Two quiz questions come from this.

question.text: Which group do jellyfish and corals belong to?
question.explain: Cnidarians. The giveaway is the stinging cells, which is what the group is named for.

cards.title: Arthropods outnumber everything else
cards.text: Insects, spiders, crabs, centipedes. More than three-quarters of all known animal species sit in this one group.
points: **Jointed legs** — that is what the name means.
**Exoskeleton** — the skeleton is on the outside.
**They have to moult** to grow, which is the cost.
**Small size** is a large part of why there are so many.

cards.title: Cars are built both ways too
cards.text: This is not a loose comparison. It is the same engineering choice, made for the same reasons.
points: **Body-on-frame** — an inner chassis carries the load. Endoskeleton.
**Monocoque** — the outer shell carries it. Exoskeleton.
**The shell is lighter and stiffer** at small sizes.
**It is harder to make big.** Same as an insect.

options: A skeleton on the outside of the body
A skeleton that never stops growing
A backbone made of many parts
question.explain: Outside. That is why arthropods have to moult: the armour cannot grow with them.

cards.title: Death Stranding wears its skeleton outside
cards.text: That game uses the real word correctly. An exoskeleton is a frame worn outside that carries load for you.
points: **Your skeleton is inside**, holding you up.
**A crab's is outside**, doing the same job.
**Wearing one** is borrowing the arthropod design.
**The game named it right.**

question.text: Most animal species on earth are vertebrates.
question.explain: False. Around 95% are invertebrates, and most of those are arthropods.

terms.def: An animal with a backbone. Five classes.
An animal with no backbone. About 95% of all animal species.
Body temperature follows the surroundings. Fish, amphibians, reptiles.
Body temperature held steady from inside. Birds and mammals only.
A skeleton on the outside of the body, as in arthropods.
A skeleton inside the body, as in all vertebrates.
Shedding an outgrown exoskeleton so a bigger one can form.
Jointed legs and an exoskeleton. Insects, spiders, crabs.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Backbone or no backbone.** That is the split.
**Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.**
**Only birds and mammals are warm-blooded.**
**Arthropods are most of the animal kingdom.**

quiz.text: What makes an animal a vertebrate?
options: It gives birth to live young
quiz.explain: The backbone, and nothing else. Fish and mammals are both vertebrates and share almost nothing else.
quiz.objective: Explain what makes an animal a vertebrate

quiz.text: Which class has moist skin and starts life in water with gills?
quiz.explain: Amphibians. Tadpoles have gills and grow lungs later, which is why the group is named for two lives.
quiz.objective: Name the five vertebrate classes and one feature of each

quiz.text: Which class has feathers and hollow bones?
quiz.explain: Birds. Hollow bones save weight, which matters a great deal if you fly.
quiz.objective: Name the five vertebrate classes and one feature of each

quiz.text: All mammals give birth to live young.
quiz.explain: False. The platypus and the echidna lay eggs and are still mammals, because they have hair and produce milk.
quiz.objective: Name the five vertebrate classes and one feature of each

quiz.explain: Only those two hold their own temperature. The other three take it from the surroundings.
quiz.objective: Name the five vertebrate classes and one feature of each

quiz.text: Snails, clams and octopuses belong to which group?
quiz.explain: Molluscs. Soft body, very often with a shell — though the octopus has given its shell up.
quiz.objective: Name six invertebrate groups and give an example of each

quiz.text: Starfish and sea urchins belong to which group?
quiz.explain: Echinoderms — spiny skin, built around a circle, and every one of them lives in the sea.
quiz.objective: Name six invertebrate groups and give an example of each

quiz.explain: Cnidarians: jellyfish, corals and sea anemones. The stinging cells are what define the group.
quiz.objective: Name six invertebrate groups and give an example of each

quiz.text: What is the name for a skeleton on the OUTSIDE of the body?
quiz.explain: An exoskeleton. Exo- means outside, which is the whole word.
quiz.objective: Explain the difference between an exoskeleton and an endoskeleton

quiz.text: Why does an arthropod have to moult?
options: Its exoskeleton cannot grow with it
It gets too heavy to move
The old skeleton loses its colour
quiz.explain: The armour is rigid, so growing means leaving it behind and making a bigger one.
quiz.objective: Explain the difference between an exoskeleton and an endoskeleton

quiz.text: Which is the largest animal group by number of species?
quiz.explain: Arthropods, by a very long way. More than three-quarters of all known animal species.
quiz.objective: Explain why arthropods are the largest animal group

quiz.text: About 95% of animal species have no backbone.
quiz.explain: True. Vertebrates get the attention because we are one, but by species count they are tiny.
quiz.objective: Explain why arthropods are the largest animal group

teacher.summary: Week 6 Science covers vertebrates and invertebrates, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. It is a classification topic, so it is taught as a set of decisions rather than a set of lists: one question for the top-level split, one identifying feature per class, and one group that accounts for most of the answer. The two figures carry the two lists so the cards can spend their space on the reasoning. The car card is not an analogy for its own sake — body-on-frame against monocoque is the same engineering trade-off as endoskeleton against exoskeleton, including the reason both shells struggle at large sizes.
discussion: Ask him to name an animal and work out its class out loud. Doing five in a row fixes the features better than reading them.
Ask why a snake can eat once a month and he cannot. Holding your own temperature is expensive, and that is the answer.
Ask why there are no insects the size of a dog. The exoskeleton and moulting between them explain it.
Ask which half of the animal kingdom he would have guessed was bigger before the lesson.
teacher.extension: Have him classify every animal he can see in one photograph or one aquarium visit, down to group. The invertebrates are the harder half and there will be more of them.
misconceptions: 'Cold-blooded means the animal is cold.' It means its temperature follows the surroundings. A lizard on a hot rock is warmer than you.
'All mammals give birth to live young.' The platypus and echidna lay eggs and are still mammals.
'Most animals are vertebrates.' Around 95% of animal species have no backbone at all.
'An exoskeleton is just armour.' It is the skeleton. Everything attaches to it, which is why moulting is so risky.
